sentences.text: An electricity pole is situated adjacent to the plaintiff's residence.

On 30.06.2016, at approximately 1:45 PM, while the plaintiff and his mother were standing on the balcony of their residence, a sudden gust of wind caused an electric current-- transmitted through live, loosely hanging electric wires from the said pole--to come into contact with the iron grill of the balcony.
As a result, the grill became electrified, and the plaintiff suffered an electric shock and was consequently electrocuted.
3 The plaintiff's mother, upon witnessing the incident, grasped the wooden door of the balcony with one hand and, with the other, managed to pull the plaintiff away from the electrified grill.
However, by that time, the plaintiff had lost consciousness and his mother also sustained a minor electric shock.
4 The plaintiff's maternal grandfather immediately transported both the plaintiff and his mother to Gandhi Hospital, where they were administered medical treatment.

The plaintiff's mother was discharged on the same day, while the plaintiff was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) due to serious burn injuries sustained on his right arm and the right side of his head caused by the high voltage current.
As the plaintiff's condition continued to deteriorate, he was transferred to PGI Chandigarh for advanced treatment.

Ultimately,
the severity of the injuries necessitated the amputation of the plaintiff's right arm and disarticulation at the right shoulder.

The plaintiff has since been certified as suffering from 94%
permanent locomotor disability.

He remains under ongoing medical supervision at PGI Chandigarh,
requiring regular visits by his mother and other family members.

5 On 30.06.2016, the plaintiff's paternal grandfather contacted the Police Control Room (PCR),

30.1 The issues under consideration are interrelated in nature and, therefore, are being adjudicated upon collectively.

30.2 It is an undisputed fact that on the afternoon of 30.09.2016, at approximately 1:45 PM, the plaintiff suffered an electric shock while standing in the balcony of his residence, as a result of which he sustained severe burn injuries.

It is further not in dispute that the plaintiff sustained burn injuries on the right side of his scalp and that his right shoulder had to be disarticulated, resulting in the complete amputation of his right arm from the shoulder.
This injury has led to a permanent 94% 'Locomotor Disability', as evidenced by Ex. PW1/C.
It is also not contested that the balcony's iron grill became electrified due to electrical current transmitted from the nearby electricity pole adjacent to the plaintiff's residence.
30.3 The plaintiff has asserted that the high-tension cables on the said pole were hanging loosely and, due to the wind, came into contact with the iron grill of the balcony.

In contrast, the defendants have denied the existence of any loose wires and have attributed the cause of the incident to the illegal extension of the balcony by the owner of the premises, which allegedly brought the structure in close proximity to the pole that had existed since before the construction of the building.
It has also been contended that the incident was an 'Act of God', given that 30.09.2016 was a windy day.

30.4 Learned counsel for Defendant Nos.1 and 2 have further argued that the plaintiff's residence was constructed without a sanctioned building plan, and that the registered sale deed does not mention any balcony, indicating that it may have been constructed subsequently.
It has also been contended that no prior notice or complaint regarding any loose electrical cables was ever served upon the defendants.
30.5 This latter argument is devoid of merit.
The plaintiff's residence is located within a duly sanctioned colony and was purchased pursuant to a registered sale deed.
The plaintiff's mother has deposed that no additional construction was undertaken by her following the purchase.
Hence, the burden of proving that the balcony was illegally constructed or was added post-purchase lay upon the defendants.
No credible evidence has been led by the defendants in this regard.

Furthermore, Defendant Nos.1 and 2, being responsible for the maintenance of electric poles, cables, and related infrastructure, cannot evade liability by contending that they were not informed about defects or deficiencies in maintenance.

30.6 Even assuming, arguendo, that the cables were not loose prior to the incident,
this Court is not persuaded by the stand taken by the defendants.
PW1 has testified that there was no rainfall on the day in question.
None of the defendants have pleaded that there was rainfall or stormy weather on that day.

sentences.text:
Section 53 of the Act authorises the appropriate Electricity Authority--in this case, BSES--to implement measures aimed at protecting the public from hazards arising out of the generation, transmission,
distribution, and use of electricity, including the proper installation and maintenance of electrical lines and equipment to prevent personal injury or property damage.

In addition, Rule 29 of the Indian Electricity Rules, 1956 mandates that all electrical apparatus must be of sufficient mechanical strength and must be installed, protected,
and maintained in a manner that ensures public safety.
Rule 46 of the said Rules further requires periodic inspection and testing of such installations.
These statutory duties are the exclusive responsibility of the electricity authority, namely, BSES. 30.8
Given that the plaintiff, a six-year-old child, and his mother were standing in the balcony at the time, it can be reasonably inferred that the weather was not extreme or stormy.

The defendants, who bear statutory responsibility for the safety and maintenance of high-tension electrical lines, cannot seek to disclaim liability by asserting that the wires became loose due to mere wind.
Such a defence is self-incriminating and indicative of gross negligence and failure to comply with the obligations imposed by the Electricity Act and the Indian Electricity Rules. 30.9

While it is true that the plaintiff's second-floor balcony was situated in close proximity to the electricity pole, this fact alone does not establish negligence,
contributory or otherwise, on the part of the plaintiff, his family, or the original builder of the house.
The electrification of the iron grill was not caused merely by the balcony's proximity to the pole, but rather due to the dislodgement of a live high-tension wire from its proper position.
Once the wire came loose, it could have fallen on any individual present on the ground or first floor or even on pedestrians below.
The potential hazard was not limited to the second-floor balcony but was, in fact, a broader threat arising from the defendants' failure to properly maintain critical electrical infrastructure.

"Though there is no statutory definition, in common parlance 'negligence' is categorised as either composite or contributory.

sentences.text: It is first necessary to find out what is a negligent act.

Negligence is omission of duty caused either by an omission to do something which a reasonable man guided upon those considerations who ordinarily by reason of conduct of human affairs would do or obligated to, or by doing something which a prudent or reasonable man would not do.

Negligence does not always mean absolute carelessness, but want of such a degree of care as is required in Karanveer Singh vs Bses Rajdhani Power Ltd And Ors on 26 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/127274554/
9 particular circumstances.

sentences.text: Negligence is failure to observe, for the protection of the interests of another person, the degree of care, precaution and vigilance which the circumstances justly demand, whereby such other person suffers injury.
The idea of negligence and duty are strictly correlative.
Negligence means either subjectively a careless state of mind, or objectively careless conduct.
Negligence is not an absolute term, but is a relative one; it is rather a comparative term.
No absolute standard can be fixed and no mathematically exact formula can be laid down by which negligence or lack of it can be infallibly measured in a given case.

What constitutes negligence varies under different conditions and in determining whether negligence exists in a particular case, or whether a mere act or course of conduct amounts to negligence, all the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances have to be taken into account.
It is absence of care according to circumstances.
To determine whether an act would be or would not be negligent, it is relevant to determine if any reasonable man would foresee that the act would cause damage or not.
The omission to do what the law obligates or even the failure to do anything in a manner, mode or method envisaged by law would equally and per se
constitute negligence on the part of such person.
If the answer is in the affirmative, it is a negligent act.
Where an accident is due to negligence of both parties, substantially there would be contributory negligence and both would be blamed.

In a case of contributory negligence, the crucial question on which liability depends would be whether either party could, by exercise of reasonable care, have avoided the consequence of other's negligence.
Whichever party could have avoided the consequence of other's negligence would be liable for the accident.

If a person's negligent act or omission was the proximate and immediate cause of death, the fact that the person suffering injury was himself negligent and also contributed to the accident or other circumstances by which the injury was caused would not afford a defence to the other.
Contributory negligence is applicable solely to the conduct of a plaintiff.

It means that there has been an act or omission on the part of the plaintiff which has materially contributed to the damage,
the act or omission being of such a nature that it may properly be described as negligence, although negligence is not given its usual meaning.
(See Charlesworth on Negligence, 3rd Edn. Para 328)..."

sentences.text: Moreover, the electricity pole had been in place since 2004-2005.

It is an established practice--also acknowledged by D1W1--that before sanctioning a new electricity connection, Defendant No.1 conducts both commercial and technical feasibility assessments through a Technical Feasibility Engineer via a physical site inspection.
D1W1 further conceded that no objections or deficiencies were recorded in the inspection report for the plaintiff's premises.

30.13 In light of these facts, the reliance placed by the defendants on cautionary public notices published in newspapers, or on the installation of a "danger board" affixed to the pole, is misplaced and unavailing.
The premises in question had been deemed suitable for electrification by the competent authority.

If, indeed, the proximity of the balcony to the high-tension pole posed a risk,
the question arises: why was the electricity connection sanctioned in the first place?

Furthermore, if the allegations regarding illegal extension were valid, why was no action initiated under the warnings mentioned in the public notices, particularly after the site had been physically inspected by Defendant No.1's engineer?

30.14 Learned Counsel for Defendant No.1 has argued that the responsibility for carrying out inspections for new connections lies with the AMC contractor--in this case, Defendant No.2--and has placed reliance on the word "connections" appearing in Clause 4.0 of the AMC agreement (Ex.
D1W1/E).
However, this argument is untenable.
A plain reading of this clause, particularly the opening paragraph of page 9, clearly excludes new connections and meter installations from the scope of the AMC contract.
Therefore, the responsibility for such inspections cannot be shifted to Defendant No.2. 30.15

The negligence in maintenance is further evidenced by the fact that, shortly after the incident, Defendant No.1 installed an iron angle on the high-tension pole in order to increase the distance between the pole and the plaintiff's residence.

Given that the plaintiff, a six-year-old child, and his mother were standing in the balcony at the time, it can be reasonably inferred that the weather was not extreme or stormy.
The defendants, who bear statutory responsibility for the safety and maintenance of high-tension electrical lines, cannot seek to disclaim liability by asserting that the wires became loose due to mere wind.
Such a defence is self-incriminating and indicative of gross negligence and failure to comply with the obligations imposed by the Electricity Act and the Indian Electricity Rules. 30.9
While it is true that the plaintiff's second-floor balcony was situated in close proximity to the electricity pole, this fact alone does not establish negligence,
contributory or otherwise, on the part of the plaintiff, his family, or the original builder of the house.
The electrification of the iron grill was not caused merely by the balcony's proximity to the pole, but rather due to the dislodgement of a live high-tension wire from its proper position.
Once the wire came loose, it could have fallen on any individual present on the ground or first floor or even on pedestrians below.
The potential hazard was not limited to the second-floor balcony but was, in fact, a broader threat arising from the defendants' failure to properly maintain critical electrical infrastructure.
Negligence is not an absolute term, but is a relative one; it is rather a comparative term.

It was incumbent upon Defendant No.1 to have taken all reasonable and necessary precautions in advance to prevent such incidents.

It must be underscored that the supply of electricity is an inherently hazardous activity, and the margin for error must be nil.

The doctrine of strict liability postulates that a party may be held liable for the consequences of its actions or omissions, even in the absence of proven negligence, where the activity in question is inherently dangerous and the risk of harm to others is foreseeable.

Even assuming that all such measures have been adopted, a person undertaking an activity involving hazardous or risky exposure to human life, is liable under law of torts to compensate for the injury suffered by any other person, irrespective of any negligence or carelessness on the part of the managers of such undertakings.
The basis of such liability is the foreseeable risk inherent in the very nature of such activity.
The liability cast on such person is known, in law, as "strict liability".
It differs from the liability which arises on account of the negligence or fault in this way i.e. the concept of negligence comprehends that the foreseeable harm could be avoided by taking reasonable precautions.
If the defendant did all that which could be done for avoiding the harm he cannot be held liable when the action is based on any negligence attributed.
But such consideration is not relevant in cases of strict liability where the defendant is held liable irrespective of whether he could have avoided the particular harm by taking precautions.
The principle of liability without fault was enunciated in Ryland v. Fletcher,
